rv.q: Instructions for Correct Assembly begins by advertising its cleverness – and goes on to be far cleverer and more penetrating.

‘Glass eye, grey-green’ and ‘toenails, three’ suggest this is no IKEA-based undertaking. Instead the couple is assembling a fully automated boy, Jan (Brian Vernel), to replace their late son Nick (also Vernel). The finish they’ve selected for Jan is ‘white and polite’; Eccleshare is a dab hand at the stinging one-liner.

Harry points at a picture and says to his wife, Max: “I thought we could have a go at it together. You know like we did the upstairs bed?” Max looks pleased and Harry nods: “You had natural flat-pack talent.” Max looks even more pleased: “You said I was the Susan Boyle of DIY.”
If the script finally runs out of battery, this is a lively new play bustling with ideas and laughs.
The grief, though, to my mind is not as well handled.
The meandering script has an error that any competent producer ought to spot: a lack of conflict between the parents.
Instructions for Correct Assembly is an interesting and inventive piece of theatre.
Thomas Eccleshare has written an amusing Sci-Fi satire on parental expectation and parental disappointment.
Instructions For Correct Assembly is never quite as alarming as it should be.
This is an enjoyably cartoon critique of everyday conformity, but don’t expect anything else.

cn.t: Eccleshare's sci-fi satire about parents building a flat-pack child earns praise for its clever premise, strong performances, and striking design, though some critics find it derivative and thin on substance beyond the initial concept.
